newsitem.title: FRANCE: French explorer cracks mystery of gold-digging ants.
newsitem.headline: French explorer cracks mystery of gold-digging ants.

text.p: A French explorer said on Tuesday he had cracked the 2,500-year-old mystery of "gold-digging ants", saying they were in fact marmots burrowing in gold-bearing sands high in the Himalayas.
Frenchman Michel Peissel told Reuters he had spotted the mountain rodents on a rare expedition to the Karakoram mountains of Baltistan, a remote region disputed by India and Pakistan.

Peissel, who has been exploring the Himalayas for 36 years, said the Greek historian Herodotus first reported 25 centuries ago that natives of a mysterious region collected gold brought by "ants bigger than foxes and smaller than dogs".
"The idea that animals were delivering gold to humans was like a dream," Peissel said of the oft-disputed legend.
Alexander the Great of Greece and Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent were among many treasure hunters who had searched in vain for the ants' gold, he said.

Peissel, 59, said he was first tipped 13 years ago that the mysterious region could be the 3,500-metre-high (10,500 ft) Baltistan plain of Dansar. But he only obtained permission from Islamabad this year to visit the region, a restricted military area where Pakistani and Indian troops regularly exchange fire.
He said he observed the marmots and the presence of strata of gold-bearing sand one metre (three feet) underground.

"It is this dark gold-bearing sand that the 'mountain ants', as marmots were called in ancient Persian, brought to the surface and that the local Minaro people collected 2,500 years ago and still quite recently," Peissel said.
He said his findings vindicated Herodotus, "ending what has no doubt been the longest treasure hunt in history".
Peissel, who speaks Tibetan dialects fluently and has staged 25 expeditions to the Himalayas, discovered the source of the Mekong river in Tibet two years ago.
He reported last year discovering a previously unknown breed of small and primitive forest pony in a remote part of Tibet.
He is a Fellow of Britain's Royal Geographical Society and a member emeritus of the New York Explorers Club.
